claim: The embryonic Drosophila airway tree is roughly subdivided into two types of cells with distinct developmental potentials: a proximally located group of multipotent adult precursor cells (P-fate) and a distally located population of more differentiated cells (D-fate).
source: The embryonic Drosophila airway tree is roughly subdivided into two types of cells with distinct developmental potentials: a proximally located group of multipotent adult precursor cells (P-fate) and a distally located population of more differentiated cells (D-fate).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing differential marker expression in proximal vs distal regions throughout the manuscript.

claim: The GATA-family transcription factor Grain promotes the P-fate.
source: We show that the GATA-family transcription factor (TF) Grain promotes the P-fate and the POU-homeobox TF Ventral veinless (Vvl/Drifter/U-turned) stimulates the D-fate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing grn expression in P-fate cells and loss of P-fate markers in grn mutants (Figure 4).

claim: The POU-homeobox TF Ventral veinless (Vvl/Drifter/U-turned) stimulates the D-fate.
source: We show that the GATA-family transcription factor (TF) Grain promotes the P-fate and the POU-homeobox TF Ventral veinless (Vvl/Drifter/U-turned) stimulates the D-fate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing vvl expression in D-fate cells and expansion of P-fate markers in vvl mutants (Figure 3).

claim: Hedgehog and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling cooperate with Vvl to drive the D-fate at the expense of the P-fate.
source: Hedgehog and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling cooperate with Vvl to drive the D-fate at the expense of the P-fate while negative regulators of either of these signaling pathways ensure P-fate specification.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction experiments showing that loss of hh and RTK components together with vvl eliminates D-fate markers (Figures 3, 5).

claim: Negative regulators of Hedgehog and RTK signaling pathways ensure P-fate specification.
source: Hedgehog and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling cooperate with Vvl to drive the D-fate at the expense of the P-fate while negative regulators of either of these signaling pathways ensure P-fate specification.
evidence: Supported by data showing that aos, aop, and Gap1 (negative regulators of RTK signaling) are required for P-fate maintenance (Figure 7).

claim: Local concentrations of Decapentaplegic/BMP, Wingless/Wnt, and Hedgehog signals differentially regulate the expression of D-factors and P-factors.
source: Local concentrations of Decapentaplegic/BMP, Wingless/Wnt, and Hedgehog signals differentially regulate the expression of D-factors and P-factors to transform an equipotent primordial field into a concentric pattern of radially different morphogenetic potentials, which gradually gives rise to the distal-proximal organization of distinct cell types in the mature airway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing effects of wg, dpp, and hh mutations on P/D fate marker expression (Figures 6, 7).

claim: The discovery of a small number of transcription factors can induce pluripotent cells.
source: The discovery of a small number of transcription factors that can induce pluripotent cells (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006) has fueled major research efforts to reveal the mechanisms biasing the choice between pluripotent/multipotent and more differentiated cell fates in vivo (O'Brien and Bilder, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: Drosophila embryos are metamerically divided along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis by mid-embryogenesis.
source: By mid-embryogenesis, Drosophila embryos are metamerically divided along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis (Ingham, 1988; Sanson, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge in Drosophila development, supported by citations to Ingham, 1988 and Sanson, 2001.

claim: Each embryonic segment is subdivided along the dorso-ventral (DV) embryo axis.
source: Each unit (segment or parasegment) is also subdivided along the dorso-ventral (DV) embryo axis (Anderson et al., 1985b; Wharton et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge in Drosophila development, supported by citations to Anderson et al., 1985b and Wharton et al., 1993.

claim: Wingless (Wg) expressed in stripes along the AP axis represses airway primordia specification.
source: For example, Wingless (Wg) expressed in stripes along the AP axis and Decapentaplegic (Dpp) expressed in the dorsal ectoderm (Figure 1B) repress the airway primordia specification (Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Isaac and Andrew, 1996 and Wilk et al., 1996, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Decapentaplegic (Dpp) expressed in the dorsal ectoderm represses airway primordia specification.
source: For example, Wingless (Wg) expressed in stripes along the AP axis and Decapentaplegic (Dpp) expressed in the dorsal ectoderm (Figure 1B) repress the airway primordia specification (Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Isaac and Andrew, 1996 and Wilk et al., 1996, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: 10 metameric groups of cells expressing Trachealess (Trh) are specified on each side of the lateral ectoderm.
source: As a result, 10 metameric groups of cells expressing a master gene, Trachealess (Trh) are specified on each side of the lateral ectoderm (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A-B showing trh expression pattern.

claim: Invagination of each primordial cluster transforms the two-dimensional (2D) shape of each cluster to 3D tubes.
source: Invagination of each primordial cluster transforms the two-dimensional (2D) shape of each cluster to 3D tubes (Figure 1C) (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1985; Turner and Mahowald, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1985 and Turner and Mahowald, 1977, and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Within the invaginated primitive sacs/tubes, the proximal cells form a narrow cord, the spiracular branch/SB (P-fate).
source: Within the invaginated primitive sacs/tubes, the proximal cells form a narrow cord, the spiracular branch/SB (P-fate) (Figure 1C, K) and stay multipotent to later proliferate and to generate many parts of the pupal/adult airways (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008, and illustrated in Figure 1C, K.

claim: P-fate cells stay multipotent to later proliferate and to generate many parts of the pupal/adult airways.
source: Within the invaginated primitive sacs/tubes, the proximal cells form a narrow cord, the spiracular branch/SB (P-fate) (Figure 1C, K) and stay multipotent to later proliferate and to generate many parts of the pupal/adult airways (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008.

claim: The more distal parts of D-fate cells extend six primary branches.
source: Within the remaining distal cells (D-fate), the more distal parts achieve a series of morphogenetic events, extending six primary branches, fusing with branches from neighboring metameres and supplying oxygen directly to the target cells (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b), while the more proximal parts (transverse connectives/TC) connect SB with the primary branches (Figure 1C, K).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b, and illustrated in Figure 1C, K.

claim: D-fate cells fuse with branches from neighboring metameres.
source: Within the remaining distal cells (D-fate), the more distal parts achieve a series of morphogenetic events, extending six primary branches, fusing with branches from neighboring metameres and supplying oxygen directly to the target cells (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b), while the more proximal parts (transverse connectives/TC) connect SB with the primary branches (Figure 1C, K).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b.

claim: D-fate cells supply oxygen directly to the target cells.
source: Within the remaining distal cells (D-fate), the more distal parts achieve a series of morphogenetic events, extending six primary branches, fusing with branches from neighboring metameres and supplying oxygen directly to the target cells (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b), while the more proximal parts (transverse connectives/TC) connect SB with the primary branches (Figure 1C, K).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b.

claim: Transverse connectives (TC) connect SB with the primary branches.
source: Within the remaining distal cells (D-fate), the more distal parts achieve a series of morphogenetic events, extending six primary branches, fusing with branches from neighboring metameres and supplying oxygen directly to the target cells (Manning and Krasnow, 1993; Samakovlis et al., 1996a; Samakovlis et al., 1996b), while the more proximal parts (transverse connectives/TC) connect SB with the primary branches (Figure 1C, K).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 1C, K.

claim: rhomboid (rho) is expressed in each primordium.
source: For example, rhomboid (rho) is expressed in each primordium (Bier et al., 1990) and activates dEGFR (also called torpedo or faint little ball) (Price et al., 1989; Schejter and Shilo, 1989) by generating the secreted active ligand Spitz (s-Spi) (Gabay et al., 1997; Golembo et al., 1996; Schweitzer et al., 1995b; Urban et al., 2001; Wappner et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bier et al., 1990.

claim: rhomboid activates dEGFR by generating the secreted active ligand Spitz (s-Spi).
source: For example, rhomboid (rho) is expressed in each primordium (Bier et al., 1990) and activates dEGFR (also called torpedo or faint little ball) (Price et al., 1989; Schejter and Shilo, 1989) by generating the secreted active ligand Spitz (s-Spi) (Gabay et al., 1997; Golembo et al., 1996; Schweitzer et al., 1995b; Urban et al., 2001; Wappner et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gabay et al., 1997; Golembo et al., 1996; Schweitzer et al., 1995b; Urban et al., 2001; Wappner et al., 1997.

claim: Activated dEGFR instructs the cytoskeletal changes that coordinate invagination.
source: Activated dEGFR instructs the cytoskeletal changes that coordinate invagination (Brodu and Casanova, 2006; Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Llimargas and Casanova, 1999; Nishimura et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brodu and Casanova, 2006; Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Llimargas and Casanova, 1999; Nishimura et al., 2007.

claim: Branchless (Bnl)/dFGF is expressed in patches of surrounding tissues to guide primary branching.
source: Branchless (Bnl)/dFGF is expressed in patches of surrounding tissues to guide primary branching (Sutherland et al., 1996) by activating Breathless (Btl)/dFGFR on the airway cells (Klambt et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sutherland et al., 1996.

claim: Branchless (Bnl)/dFGF guides primary branching by activating Breathless (Btl)/dFGFR on the airway cells.
source: Branchless (Bnl)/dFGF is expressed in patches of surrounding tissues to guide primary branching (Sutherland et al., 1996) by activating Breathless (Btl)/dFGFR on the airway cells (Klambt et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klambt et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1996.

claim: Decapentaplegic (Dpp)/BMP, Wingless (Wg)/WNT, and Hedgehog (Hh) signals combinatorially establish different primary branch identities.
source: Apart from receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling, Decapentaplegic (Dpp)/BMP, Wingless (Wg)/WNT, and Hedgehog (Hh) signals combinatorially establish different primary branch identities (Affolter et al., 1994; Chen et al., 1998; Chihara and Hayashi, 2000; Glazer and Shilo, 2001; Llimargas, 2000; Llimargas and Lawrence, 2001; Matsuda et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Affolter et al., 1994; Chen et al., 1998; Chihara and Hayashi, 2000; Glazer and Shilo, 2001; Llimargas, 2000; Llimargas and Lawrence, 2001; Matsuda et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 1997.

claim: rho is expressed preferentially in the central and distal regions of the airway primordia before and during invagination.
source: rho is expressed preferentially in the central and distal regions of the airway primordia before and during invagination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E showing rho expression patterns.

claim: btl/dFGFR is expressed preferentially in the distal part.
source: btl/dFGFR is also expressed preferentially in the distal part (Figure 1D–E), and its expression is upregulated by Bnl/dFGF in the most distal leading cells of the primary branch tips (Figure 1E) (Ohshiro et al., 2002; Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D–E showing btl expression patterns.

claim: btl/dFGFR expression is upregulated by Bnl/dFGF in the most distal leading cells of the primary branch tips.
source: btl/dFGFR is also expressed preferentially in the distal part (Figure 1D–E), and its expression is upregulated by Bnl/dFGF in the most distal leading cells of the primary branch tips (Figure 1E) (Ohshiro et al., 2002; Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohshiro et al., 2002; Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997, and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: mAb2A12 detects the putative chitin-binding protein Gasp.
source: mAb2A12 detecting the putative chitin-biding protein Gasp (Tiklova et al., 2013) preferentially labels the distal airways during stages 14-17 (Figure 1F) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tiklova et al., 2013.

claim: mAb2A12 preferentially labels the distal airways during stages 14-17.
source: mAb2A12 detecting the putative chitin-biding protein Gasp (Tiklova et al., 2013) preferentially labels the distal airways during stages 14-17 (Figure 1F) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samakovlis et al., 1996a and illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: unpaired (upd) is expressed only in the proximal SB cells from stage 12 on.
source: On the other hand, unpaired (upd), a ligand activating the JAK/STAT signaling is expressed only in the proximal SB cells from stage 12 on (Figure 1G–I) (Harrison et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harrison et al., 1998 and illustrated in Figure 1G–I.

claim: unpaired (upd) is a ligand activating the JAK/STAT signaling.
source: On the other hand, unpaired (upd), a ligand activating the JAK/STAT signaling is expressed only in the proximal SB cells from stage 12 on (Figure 1G–I) (Harrison et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harrison et al., 1998.

claim: From stage 13 onwards, the SB cells show stronger expression of the P0144 enhancer trap marker.
source: From stage 13 onwards, the SB cells also show stronger expression of the P0144 enhancer trap marker (Figure 1E,F,I) (http://flyview.uni-muenster.de).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 1E,F,I.

claim: The 10th tracheal primordium (Tr10) does not establish the P0144-positive P-fate due to the high level of a Hox protein Abdominal-B (AbdB) in this part of the embryo.
source: Compared to the anterior metameres, the 10th tracheal primordium (Tr10) does not establish the P0144-postive P-fate due to the high level of a Hox protein Abdominal-B (AbdB) in this part of the embryo (Figure 1F, J), (Celniker et al., 1989; Matsuda et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Celniker et al., 1989; Matsuda et al., 2015, and illustrated in Figure 1F, J.

claim: In trh mutants, both the D-fate marker and the P-fate marker expressions are lost.
source: In trh mutants, both the D-fate marker (Chung et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2001; Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997; Zelzer and Shilo, 2000) and the P-fate marker expressions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1U, V) are lost.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2001; Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997; Zelzer and Shilo, 2000, and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1U, V.

claim: pointed (pnt) is a general transcriptional target and mediator of RTK signaling.
source: pointed (pnt) is a general transcriptional target and mediator of RTK signaling (Brunner et al., 1994; Klambt, 1993; O'Neill et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brunner et al., 1994; Klambt, 1993; O'Neill et al., 1994.

claim: rho induces pnt expression in the central parts of the airway primordia.
source: rho induces pnt expression in the central parts of the airway primordia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–O) and btl/dFGFR upregulates pnt expression in the tips of the primary branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–O) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–O.

claim: btl/dFGFR upregulates pnt expression in the tips of the primary branches.
source: rho induces pnt expression in the central parts of the airway primordia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–O) and btl/dFGFR upregulates pnt expression in the tips of the primary branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–O) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samakovlis et al., 1996a and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–O.

claim: Markers of the central parts of the airway primordia (pnt-lacZ and btl-CD8-GFP) become preferentially expressed in the distal part of the airway tree.
source: Markers of the central parts of the airway primordia (pnt-lacZ and btl-CD8-GFP) become preferentially expressed in the distal part of the airway tree (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N–O).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N–O.

claim: hairy (h) expression in the airway primordia is confined to the dorso-central part.
source: Similarly, hairy (h) expression in the airway primordia (Carroll et al., 1988; Hooper et al., 1989; Zhan et al., 2010) is confined to the dorso-central part (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P) and its reporter (h-lacZ) becomes active in most of the DB, VB, and DT cells but not in TC, SB nor in ventral branches (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carroll et al., 1988; Hooper et al., 1989; Zhan et al., 2010, and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1P.

claim: h-lacZ becomes active in most of the DB, VB, and DT cells but not in TC, SB nor in ventral branches.
source: Similarly, hairy (h) expression in the airway primordia (Carroll et al., 1988; Hooper et al., 1989; Zhan et al., 2010) is confined to the dorso-central part (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P) and its reporter (h-lacZ) becomes active in most of the DB, VB, and DT cells but not in TC, SB nor in ventral branches (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q) (Samakovlis et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samakovlis et al., 1996a and illustrated in Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: salm labels the dorsal part of the airway primordia.
source: In contrast, salm labels the dorsal part of the airway primordia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1R), (Kuhnlein and Schuh, 1996) and salm-gal4 driven UAS-GFP marks DB and DT, and parts of TC and SB in the airways (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S–T).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuhnlein and Schuh, 1996 and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1R.

claim: salm-gal4 driven UAS-GFP marks DB and DT, and parts of TC and SB in the airways.
source: In contrast, salm labels the dorsal part of the airway primordia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1R), (Kuhnlein and Schuh, 1996) and salm-gal4 driven UAS-GFP marks DB and DT, and parts of TC and SB in the airways (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S–T).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S–T.

claim: The dorso-peripheral sector of each primordium, which is positive for salm but lacking h, composes half of the proximal SB cells in the airway tree.
source: These results suggest that the dorso-peripheral sector of each primordium, which is positive for salm but lacking h, composes half of the proximal SB cells in the airway tree.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of salm and h markers shown in the figures.

claim: Around the completion of invagination, the P-fate marker upd is enriched in a horseshoe-like peripheral ring.
source: Consistently, around the completion of invagination, the P-fate marker upd is enriched in a horseshoe-like peripheral ring (Figure 1G)(Harrison et al., 1998), which eventually marks the SB cells at stage 12 (Figure 1H,I,K).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harrison et al., 1998 and illustrated in Figure 1G.

claim: The gene expression analysis suggests a fate map of the airway primordia, where the centro-peripheral axis inversely correlates both with the ordered pattern of tracheal cell invagination and the PD axis of airway branching.
source: Collectively, the gene expression analysis suggests a fate map of the airway primordia, where the centro-peripheral axis inversely correlates both with the ordered pattern of tracheal cell invagination (Brodu and Casanova, 2006; Nishimura et al., 2007) and the PD axis of airway branching (Figure 1C,K).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns shown in the figures, supported by citations to Brodu and Casanova, 2006; Nishimura et al., 2007.

claim: In btl/dFGFR mutants, apoptotic staining in the distal cells increases from stage 12.
source: In btl/dFGFR mutants, where active branch extension does not occur, apoptotic staining in the distal cells increases from stage 12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that btl/dFGFR signaling directly or indirectly suppresses apoptosis of the distal airways.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: btl/dFGFR signaling directly or indirectly suppresses apoptosis of the distal airways.
source: In btl/dFGFR mutants, where active branch extension does not occur, apoptotic staining in the distal cells increases from stage 12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that btl/dFGFR signaling directly or indirectly suppresses apoptosis of the distal airways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased apoptosis observed in btl mutants.

claim: In dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants, massive cell death staining accompanies loss of most tracheal cells compared to either single mutant.
source: In dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants, massive cell death staining accompanies loss of most tracheal cells compared to either single mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Suppression of apoptosis by removing pro-apoptotic genes using Df(H99) partially restores the survival of tracheal cells in dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants.
source: Suppression of apoptosis by removing pro-apoptotic genes using Df(H99) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) (White et al., 1994) or by transgenic expression of the apoptosis inhibitor, DIAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) (Hay et al., 1995) partially restores the survival of tracheal cells in dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 1994 and Hay et al., 1995, and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J.

claim: Transgenic expression of the apoptosis inhibitor, DIAP partially restores the survival of tracheal cells in dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants.
source: Suppression of apoptosis by removing pro-apoptotic genes using Df(H99) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) (White et al., 1994) or by transgenic expression of the apoptosis inhibitor, DIAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) (Hay et al., 1995) partially restores the survival of tracheal cells in dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 1994 and Hay et al., 1995, and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J.

claim: dEGFR and Btl/dFGFR cooperate to suppress apoptosis in the airway cells.
source: Thus, dEGFR and Btl/dFGFR cooperate to suppress apoptosis in the airway cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing enhanced apoptosis in double mutants and rescue by apoptosis inhibitors.

claim: In bnl/dFGF mutants, the feedback upregulation of the D-fate marker btl/dFGFR is lost in the tips of the primary branches.
source: In bnl/dFGF mutants, the feedback upregulation of the D-fate marker btl/dFGFR is lost in the tips of the primary branches (Figure 2A,B) (Ohshiro et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohshiro et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 2A,B.

claim: In bnl/dFGF mutants, the distal part of the invaginated stump retains the mab2A12 signal.
source: However, the distal part of the invaginated stump retains the mab2A12 signal (Lee et al., 1996) and the basal btl/dFGFR expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 1996 and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of the P-fate markers (upd and P0144-lacZ) in btl/dFGFR mutants remains largely comparable to the wild type.
source: Similarly, expression of the P-fate markers (upd and P0144-lacZ) in btl/dFGFR mutants remains largely comparable to the wild type (Figure 2E–F, I–J, M).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2E–F, I–J, M.

claim: Btl/dFGFR signaling does not play a major role in the P-D discrimination.
source: These results suggest that Btl/dFGFR signaling does not play a major role in the P-D discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that P-fate markers are largely unaffected in btl mutants.

claim: In rho mutants, the refinement of upd expression to the primordia periphery is retarded.
source: In rho mutants, however, the refinement of upd expression to the primordia periphery is retarded (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,L), and the expression domains of upd and P0144-lacZ become expanded (Figure 2G, K, M).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,L and Figure 2G, K, M.

claim: In rho mutants, the expression domains of upd and P0144-lacZ become expanded.
source: In rho mutants, however, the refinement of upd expression to the primordia periphery is retarded (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,L), and the expression domains of upd and P0144-lacZ become expanded (Figure 2G, K, M).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2G, K, M.

claim: In rho mutants, the domain of btl-expressing cells is decreased.
source: Correspondingly, the domain of btl-expressing cells is decreased (Figure 2C) suggesting that the rho-mediated dEGFR signaling drives the D-fate selection at the expense of the P-fate.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: The rho-mediated dEGFR signaling drives the D-fate selection at the expense of the P-fate.
source: Correspondingly, the domain of btl-expressing cells is decreased (Figure 2C) suggesting that the rho-mediated dEGFR signaling drives the D-fate selection at the expense of the P-fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reciprocal changes in D-fate and P-fate markers in rho mutants.

claim: In rho bnl/dFGF double mutants, btl expression is further reduced or even lost in some segments.
source: In rho bnl/dFGF double mutants, btl expression is further reduced or even lost in some segments (Figure 2D).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: In rho btl/dFGFR double mutants, mab2A12/Gasp becomes reduced or undetectable in some segments, accompanied by a concomitant increase of the proximal P0144-lacZ expression domain.
source: Correspondingly, in rho btl/dFGFR double mutants, another D-fate marker mab2A12/Gasp becomes reduced or undetectable in some segments, accompanied by a concomitant increase of the proximal P0144-lacZ expression domain (Figure 2L, N).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2L, N.

claim: P0144-lacZ expression is increased in pnt mutants.
source: Consistent with the phenotypes of rho btl/dFGFR mutants, P0144-lacZ expression is also increased in pnt mutants, (Figure 2M, Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 2M, Figure 2—figure supplement 1P.

claim: dEGFR signaling in cooperation with btl/dFGFR signaling promotes the D-fate selection at the expense of the P-fate partly through pnt.
source: Taken together, we conclude that dEGFR signaling in cooperation with btl/dFGFR signaling promotes the D-fate selection at the expense of the P-fate partly through pnt (Figure 2O).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are additional inputs in the D fate selection, independent of RTK signaling downstream of dEGFR and btl/dFGFR.
source: The residual weak expression of the D-fate markers in rho btl or dEGFR btl/dFGFR double mutants (Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M–O) suggests additional inputs in the D fate selection, independent of RTK signaling downstream of dEGFR and btl/dFGFR (Figure 2O).
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual D-fate marker expression in double mutants, illustrated in Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M–O.

claim: In vvl mutants, expression of the D-fate markers rho and btl is reduced.
source: We confirmed that in vvl mutants, expression of the D-fate markers rho and btl is reduced (Figure 3A, B, E, F).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 3A, B, E, F.

claim: In vvl mutants, mAb2A12 staining is almost diminished in the residual distal branches.
source: Moreover, mAb2A12 staining is almost diminished (Figure 3N, O) in the residual distal branches, which is restored by UAS-vvl driven with btl-gal4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 3N, O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1T.

claim: Loss of mAb2A12 staining in vvl mutants is restored by UAS-vvl driven with btl-gal4.

claim: In vvl mutants, the expression of the P-fate marker upd is expanded to the distal branches at stage 12.

claim: vvl promotes the D-fate at the expense of the P-fate.

source: This indicates that vvl promotes the D-fate at the expense of the P-fate, and a part of this function may be achieved through vvl-dependent expression of rho and btl.

claim: In wild type, vvl expression is enriched in the distal trachea.

claim: vvl itself is a D-fate marker.
source: In wild type, vvl expression is enriched in the distal trachea, indicating that vvl itself is a D-fate marker (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distal enrichment of vvl expression.

claim: In hh mutants, vvl expression is variably decreased or lost.

claim: In hh mutants, expression of the D-fate markers rho and btl is variably decreased or lost.
source: Consistently, expression of the D-fate markers rho and btl is also variably decreased or lost in hh mutants (Figure 3C,G, in 6 out of 26 embryos for btl expression).

claim: In hh mutants, expression of the P-fate marker upd is expanded and sometimes occupies the whole trachea in some segments.

claim: Hh signals from the anterior border of the airway primordia to orient the P/D fate selection toward the D-fate direction.

claim: In the absence of both hh and vvl, although expression of the D-fate markers rho and btl is variably detected in the primordia, btl expression is completely absent later.

claim: In hh vvl double mutants, the expression of P-fate markers expands to all tracheal cells.
source: Correspondingly, the expression of P-fate markers expands to all tracheal cells (Figure 3M,Q).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 3M,Q.

claim: Hh and Vvl cooperatively drive the D fate selection, partly through the activation of dEGFR and btl/dFGFR signaling in the central part of the primordium and in the distal branches.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Hh and Vvl cooperatively drive the D fate selection, partly through the activation of dEGFR and btl/dFGFR signaling in the central part of the primordium and in the distal branches.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: grn is preferentially expressed in the peripheral parts of the airway primordia from stage 11 on.
source: We revealed the GATA-family TF Grn (Brown and Castelli-Gair Hombria, 2000; Garces and Thor, 2006; Lin et al., 1995) as the P-fate promoting factor. grn is preferentially expressed in the peripheral parts of the airway primordia from stage 11 on (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: At stage 13, the P-fate cells of the SB and the overlying lateral ectoderm are positive for grn.
source: At stage 13, the P-fate cells of the SB and the overlying lateral ectoderm are positive for grn (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: grn expression is repressed in the D-cells by the D-fate determinants, hh, vvl, and RTKs.
source: grn expression is repressed in the D-cells by the D-fate determinants, hh, vvl, and RTKs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G), while grn expression in the lateral ectoderm is largely intact in the absence of tracheal cells in upd or trh mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: grn expression in the lateral ectoderm is largely intact in the absence of tracheal cells in upd or trh mutants.
source: grn expression is repressed in the D-cells by the D-fate determinants, hh, vvl, and RTKs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G), while grn expression in the lateral ectoderm is largely intact in the absence of tracheal cells in upd or trh mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I.

claim: Grn overexpression results in the upregulation of the P-fate marker P0144-lacZ in the more distal TC branches.
source: Grn overexpression results in the upregulation of the P-fate marker P0144-lacZ in the more distal TC branches (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4A–C.

claim: In grn mutants, expression of the P-fate markers upd and P0144-lacZ is lost.
source: Conversely, in grn mutants, expression of the P-fate markers upd and P0144-lacZ is lost (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), resulting in mAb2A12-positive tubes directly connecting to the epidermis.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: In grn mutants, mAb2A12-positive tubes directly connect to the epidermis.
source: Conversely, in grn mutants, expression of the P-fate markers upd and P0144-lacZ is lost (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), resulting in mAb2A12-positive tubes directly connecting to the epidermis.
evidence: This is an observation based on the staining pattern in grn mutants.

claim: In grn mutants, around 10 cells are selectively lost from the TC/VB region.

evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4G showing cell counts.

claim: Halving of the airway cell number in CycA mutants does not abolish the P-fate.
source: As halving of the airway cell number in CycA mutants (Beitel and Krasnow, 2000) does not abolish the P-fate (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K), we suggest that reduction of cell number does not account for the loss of the P-fate in grn mutants.
evidence: Supported by citation to Beitel and Krasnow, 2000 and illustrated in Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Reduction of cell number does not account for the loss of the P-fate in grn mutants.
source: As halving of the airway cell number in CycA mutants (Beitel and Krasnow, 2000) does not abolish the P-fate (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K), we suggest that reduction of cell number does not account for the loss of the P-fate in grn mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with CycA mutants.

claim: arm-gal4-mediated overexpression of Trh in grn mutants does not restore the P-fate.
source: Also, arm-gal4-mediated overexpression of Trh in grn mutants does not restore the P-fate (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L.

claim: grn functions in two ways: to establish Trh expression in the P-region and to induce the P-fate marker expression.
source: These results suggest that grn functions in two ways, namely to establish Trh expression in the P-region and to induce the P-fate marker expression (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, illustrated in Figure 4K.

claim: grn is a master regulator of the P-fate.
source: Accordingly, we designate grn a master regulator of the P-fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dual functions of grn in P-fate specification.

claim: In grn hh double mutants, the P-fate marker expression is not robustly restored.
source: Compared to the control (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, J), in grn hh double- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, L) or grn rho btl triple mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, N), the P-fate marker expression is not robustly restored.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, L.

claim: In grn rho btl triple mutants, the P-fate marker expression is not robustly restored.
source: Compared to the control (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, J), in grn hh double- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, L) or grn rho btl triple mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, N), the P-fate marker expression is not robustly restored.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, N.

claim: In grn vvl double mutants, the trh expression area appears to be very much reduced.
source: In grn vvl double mutants, the trh expression area appears to be very much reduced (Figure 5F), probably because the P-fate cells depend on grn for trh expression.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5F.

claim: P-fate cells depend on grn for trh expression.
source: In grn vvl double mutants, the trh expression area appears to be very much reduced (Figure 5F), probably because the P-fate cells depend on grn for trh expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced trh expression in grn vvl double mutants.

claim: In grn vvl double mutants, weak restoration of the P-fate markers upd and P0144-lacZ is detected in the reduced area of the distal region.
source: However, in this reduced area of the distal region, we detected weak restoration of the P-fate markers upd and P0144-lacZ (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, K).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, K.

claim: There may be another factor in the distal area that promotes the P-fate when grn and vvl are inactivated.
source: These results may suggest the presence of another factor in the distal area that promotes the P-fate when grn and vvl are inactivated.
evidence: This is speculation based on the weak restoration of P-fate markers in grn vvl double mutants.

claim: The default airway cell fate is the proximal and multipotent cell fate (the P-fate).
source: Alternatively, the default airway cell fate is the proximal and multipotent cell fate (the P-fate) and an important aspect of the grn functions in P-fate selection/promotion maybe to antagonize the D-factor vvl.
evidence: This is speculation based on the restoration of P-fate in grn vvl double mutants.

claim: An important aspect of the grn functions in P-fate selection/promotion may be to antagonize the D-factor vvl.
source: Alternatively, the default airway cell fate is the proximal and multipotent cell fate (the P-fate) and an important aspect of the grn functions in P-fate selection/promotion maybe to antagonize the D-factor vvl.
evidence: This is speculation based on the genetic interactions between grn and vvl.

claim: In the absence of both the D- and P-factors, trh expression initiates at stage 10 but becomes drastically reduced by stage 12/13.
source: In the absence of both the D- and P-factors (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B), trh expression initiates at stage 10 but becomes drastically reduced by stage 12/13 (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5E–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: In the absence of both the D- and P-factors, the expression of both proximal and distal markers is almost completely eliminated.
source: In these mutants (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, H, M, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B), the expression of both proximal and distal markers is almost completely eliminated (Figure 5A–D. Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–N).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–N, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The regulators of the D- and P-fate cooperatively promote and maintain the airway cell identity defined by trh expression.
source: We conclude that the regulators of the D- and P-fate cooperatively promote and maintain the airway cell identity defined by trh expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the loss of trh expression in the absence of both D- and P-factors.

claim: In wg/WNT mutants, expression of the D-fate markers vvl, mab2A12, and btl expands along the AP axis to cover most, if not all lateral parts of the embryos as a single band.
source: In wg/WNT mutants, expression of the D-fate markers vvl (de Celis et al., 1995), mab2A12 (Llimargas, 2000), and btl expands along the AP axis to cover most, if not all lateral parts of the embryos as a single band (Figure 6A–B, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Celis et al., 1995 and Llimargas, 2000, and illustrated in Figure 6A–B, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In wg/WNT mutants, expression of the P-fate markers grn, upd, and P0144-lacZ expands along the AP axis, approximately forming two narrow stripes, dorsal and ventral, sandwiching the D-fate.
source: On the other hand, expression of the P-fate markers grn, upd, and P0144-lacZ also expands along the AP axis, but this time, approximately forms two narrow stripes, dorsal and ventral, sandwiching the D-fate (Figure 6C, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6C, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Wg/WNT confines both the D- and P-fates along the AP axis.
source: These results suggest that Wg/WNT confines both the D- and P-fates along the AP axis (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expansion of both D- and P-fate markers in wg mutants, illustrated in Figure 6I.

claim: In the absence of dpp, trh expression expands to the dorsal midline.
source: In the absence of dpp, trh expression expands to the dorsal midline (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, D) (Isaac and Andrew, 1996) and the cells initiate btl expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Isaac and Andrew, 1996 and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, D.

claim: In the absence of dpp, the cells initiate btl expression.
source: In the absence of dpp, trh expression expands to the dorsal midline (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, D) (Isaac and Andrew, 1996) and the cells initiate btl expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the absence of dpp, neither the D-fate nor the P-fate is established.
source: However, neither the D-fate nor the P-fate is established (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E), suggesting that Dpp also functions as a positive regulator of early airway development, in addition to its repressive effect on the earliest trh expression.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: Dpp functions as a positive regulator of early airway development, in addition to its repressive effect on the earliest trh expression.
source: However, neither the D-fate nor the P-fate is established (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E), suggesting that Dpp also functions as a positive regulator of early airway development, in addition to its repressive effect on the earliest trh expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of P/D fate specification in dpp null mutants.

claim: In dpp hypomorphs, trh expression is expanded to the dorsal midline and P/D specification is confined near the dorsal midline.
source: In dpp hypomorphs (Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F–J), trh expression is expanded to the dorsal midline and P/D specification is confined near the dorsal midline, depending on the allele severities or the residual Dpp/BMP activity in the hypomorphic conditions.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F–J.

claim: In the dorsally expanded primordia of dpphr92 homozygotes, expression of the D-factors vvl and btl is detected as stripes straddling the dorsal midline.
source: In the dorsally expanded primordia of dpphr92 homozygotes, expression of the D-factors vvl and btl is detected as stripes straddling the dorsal midline (Figure 6D–E), and P-fate marker expression typically encircles the entire airway primordium except for its anterior border (Figure 6F, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6D–E.

claim: In dpphr92 homozygotes, P-fate marker expression typically encircles the entire airway primordium except for its anterior border.
source: In the dorsally expanded primordia of dpphr92 homozygotes, expression of the D-factors vvl and btl is detected as stripes straddling the dorsal midline (Figure 6D–E), and P-fate marker expression typically encircles the entire airway primordium except for its anterior border (Figure 6F, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6F, I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2J.

claim: The loss of the P-fate markers at the anterior border in dpphr92 homozygotes could be due to the activity of the D-fate inducer Hh, which is expressed just anterior to the airway primordia.
source: The loss of the P-fate markers at the anterior border in dpphr92 homozygotes could be due to the activity of the D-fate inducer Hh, which is expressed just anterior to the airway primordia (Figure 1B) (Glazer and Shilo, 2001).
evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression pattern of Hh, supported by citation to Glazer and Shilo, 2001 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The expression of the dorsal-distal marker h-lacZ is lost in hh mutant.
source: Consistent with the Hh-dependent anterior bias of the D-fate selection, the expression of the dorsal-distal marker h-lacZ, is lost in hh mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Expression of h-lacZ is lost in rho and pnt mutants but not in btl mutants.
source: Similarly, expression of h-lacZ is lost in rho and pnt mutants but not in btl mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, C, D).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, C, D.

claim: Overactivation of Hh signaling in wg/WNT mutants expands h expression along the AP axis.
source: On the other hand, overactivation of Hh signaling in wg/WNT mutants expands h expression along the AP axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1N–Q).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1N–Q (note: the manuscript text references Figure 6—figure supplement 3N–Q, but this appears to be a typo).

claim: The graded Dpp/BMP activity controls the P/D fate selection at the dorsal border of the airway primordia.
source: Collectively, this analysis suggests that the graded Dpp/BMP activity controls the P/D fate selection at the dorsal border of the airway primordia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of dpp mutations on P/D fate selection.

claim: Wg/WNT signals impinge on the P/D-fate selection along the AP axis.
source: Wg/WNT signals impinge on the P/D-fate selection along the AP axis, while Hh modulates P/D differentiation from the anterior border.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effects of wg mutations on P/D fate selection.

claim: Hh modulates P/D differentiation from the anterior border.
source: Wg/WNT signals impinge on the P/D-fate selection along the AP axis, while Hh modulates P/D differentiation from the anterior border.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effects of hh mutations on P/D fate selection.

claim: In Df(wg) dpphr92 double mutants, the whole dorsal area of the trunk/abdominal parts of the embryo takes the airway cell fate.
source: Consistent with the predominant roles of Dpp/BMP and Wg/WNT in airway primordia specification, in Df(wg) dpphr92 double mutants, the whole dorsal area of the trunk/abdominal parts of the embryo takes the airway cell fate (Figure 6G, I).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6G, I.

claim: In Df(wg) dpphr92 double mutants, the dorsal part of the airway primordia takes the D-fate and only the ventral periphery takes the P fate.
source: In this situation, the dorsal part of the airway primordia takes the D-fate and only the ventral periphery takes the P fate (Figure 6H, I), supporting our model that Dpp/BMP and Wg/WNT are key regulators of the P/D fate selection.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 6H, I.

claim: Dpp/BMP and Wg/WNT are key regulators of the P/D fate selection.
source: In this situation, the dorsal part of the airway primordia takes the D-fate and only the ventral periphery takes the P fate (Figure 6H, I), supporting our model that Dpp/BMP and Wg/WNT are key regulators of the P/D fate selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effects of wg and dpp mutations on P/D fate selection.

claim: argos (aos) is a secreted negative feedback regulator of dEGFR signaling.

source: argos (aos) is a secreted negative feedback regulator of dEGFR signaling (Schweitzer et al., 1995a) while anterior open (aop) encodes an ETS TF that antagonizes RTK signaling (Rebay and Rubin, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rebay and Rubin, 1995.

claim: Upon activation of RTK signaling, aos is induced, while Aop is excluded from the nucleus and becomes degraded.

evidence: This is established knowledge about RTK signaling regulation.

claim: In the airway primordia, aos expression gradually expands from the center to the periphery.

claim: At early stage 12, both aos and Aop are preferentially detected in the proximal airways.
source: At early stage 12, both aos and Aop are preferentially detected in the proximal airways (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: In aop mutants, the number of cells expressing P-fate markers is very much reduced.

evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tracheal overexpression of RasV12 with btl-gal4 or trh-gal4 in an aos mutant background abolishes P0144-lacZ expression.

claim: Tracheal overexpression of s-spi with btl-gal4 or trh-gal4 in an aos mutant background abolishes P0144-lacZ expression.
source: Similar phenotypes are observed upon tracheal overexpression of RasV12 (Figure 7D) or s-spi (Figure 7E) with btl-gal4 or trh-gal4 in an aos mutant background.
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: In double mutants of aos and Gap1, expression of the P-fate markers upd and grn is variably reduced or abolished.
source: In double mutants of aos and Gap1, a GTPase-activating protein for Ras85D (Gaul et al., 1992), expression of the P-fate markers upd and grn is variably reduced or abolished (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaul et al., 1992 and illustrated in Figure 7G,H.

claim: Gap1 is a GTPase-activating protein for Ras85D.
source: In double mutants of aos and Gap1, a GTPase-activating protein for Ras85D (Gaul et al., 1992), expression of the P-fate markers upd and grn is variably reduced or abolished (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaul et al., 1992.

claim: In aos Gap1 double mutants, the expression of P0144-lacZ is lost.
source: The expression of another P fate marker P0144-lacZ is also lost (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: In aos Gap1 double mutants, the distal mAb2A12/Gasp marker staining appears on the embryo outer surface.
source: Concomitantly, the distal mAb2A12/Gasp marker staining appears on the embryo outer surface (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7E–F.

claim: aos, Gap1, and aop are parts of a negative regulatory mechanism balancing the D-fate inducing activity of RTK signaling to assure P-fate selection.

evidence: Supported by citation to Simon et al., 1991 and illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–I.

claim: vvl, hh, and RTK signaling components have essential roles as D-fate determinants.

claim: Neither the CNS midline nor btl/dFGFR are involved in the RTK overactivation observed in the aos Gap1 double mutants.
source: Thus, these results illustrate the essential roles of vvl, hh, and RTK signaling components as D-fate determinants and suggest that neither the CNS midline nor btl/dFGFR are involved in the RTK overactivation observed in the aos Gap1 double mutants.

claim: arm-gal4 mediated, ubiquitous overexpression of secreted active spitz (s-spi) results in loss of the P-fate marker P0144-lacZ.

claim: Loss of P0144-lacZ upon s-spi overexpression is suppressed by mutations of vvl, pnt, or Ras85D but not by btl, rho, or hh mutations.
source: This defect is also suppressed by mutations of vvl, pnt, or Ras85D but not by btl, rho, or hh mutations (Figure 7—figure supplement 2J–P).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2J–P.

claim: vvl has an additional essential role in dEGFR signaling other than facilitating active dEGFR ligand production.
source: This suggests that vvl has an additional essential role in dEGFR signaling other than facilitating active dEGFR ligand production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the suppression of s-spi overexpression phenotype by vvl mutation.

claim: bnl overexpression does not abolish P0144-lacZ expression.
source: In contrast to s-spi, bnl overexpression does not abolish P0144-lacZ expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1Q).
